This study examines the thermodynamics of Lee-Wick (LW) fields within the cosmological evolution of the early universe. We analyze the dynamics of a massless LW scalar field and a massive LW fermion interacting with a radiation field. Our findings indicate that LW fields can drive accelerated cosmic expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LW fermions may alter the nucleosynthesis era by modifying the expansion rate, potentially resulting in a universe where baryogenesis occurs after deuterium formation. We also investigate the thermal properties of these LW fields, concluding that massive LW fermions can cause the radiation temperature to decrease at a slower rate than in standard cosmology.

Style transfer is a rapidly evolving field in computer vision that has garnered significant attention recently. While numerous approaches exist, most rely on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to capture the stylistic features of reference images. However, CNNs are constrained by their reliance on local receptive fields, which hinders their ability to model long-range dependencies. In contrast, Vision Transformers (ViTs) utilize a self-attention mechanism to effectively encode global contextual information. This paper introduces a novel transformer-based architecture for image style transfer, leveraging the global representational power of ViTs to generate outputs that are both semantically coherent and aesthetically pleasing. Our method employs a dual-transformer framework: the first encoder processes the content image, while the second handles the style image. These encoders are paired with a decoder that synthesizes the final stylized result. We evaluated our approach on various benchmark datasets, including CelebA, ArtPics, and a custom dataset created by the authors. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our model outperforms existing CNN-based techniques.

Thermodynamic length, defined as the square root of the Fisher information, has been shown to establish a lower bound for the dissipated work in adiabatic protocols, a concept that has been experimentally validated in various quantum systems. However, the theoretical framework for this metric has been limited to scenarios where the Fisher length remains constant throughout the process. This study addresses that constraint by demonstrating that, for any system possessing a monotonic dissipation function, the rate of energy loss is minimized exclusively when the thermodynamic length is uniform. We further illustrate that this principle holds true for the erasure of information, aligning with Landauer's principle. Consequently, we experimentally verified the approach using a superconducting circuit, confirming that maintaining a constant dissipation rate necessitates a thermodynamic length that is constant.

This study examines the single production of a vector-like $T$ quark at a future high-energy linear $e^+e^-$ collider, specifically investigating the $s$-channel process $e^+e^- \to tZ$ and the $tZ$ final state. We analyze the differential cross-sections and signal-to-background ratio for various $T$ quark masses and Yukawa couplings, utilizing the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and Pythia 8.2 simulation tools. Our findings indicate that the $tZ$ final state offers a promising channel for single $T$ quark searches, with a potential discovery reach extending up to approximately 1.5 TeV at a linear $e^+e^-$ collider operating at a center-of-mass energy of 3 TeV.

This study examines the stability of inhomogeneous fluids situated within a standing acoustic field. We demonstrate that within a specific parameter range, the system exhibits a bifurcation from a steady state to a spatiotemporal pattern. This pattern is characterized by a time-periodic modulation of the inhomogeneity, which in turn drives a self-sustained streaming flow. We provide an analytical description of this flow, revealing that it closely resembles the streaming flow generated by boundary layers in a quiescent acoustic field.

This study examines weighted shifts over the complex field within generalized directed semi-trees. We establish both necessary and sufficient criteria for the analyticity of these shifts on generalized directed semi-trees and provide specific applications concerning shifts on generalized directed trees.

This study examines the generation of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs through the interaction of a $\gamma$-photon flash, produced by an ultra-intense laser operating in the $\lambda^3$ regime, with a high-Z target. The $\gamma$-photon population is derived from the laser-induced nonlinear Compton scattering of electrons within the target. The $\gamma$-photon pulse parameters are optimized to maximize the yield of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs. The analysis reveals that the yield of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs increases with higher atomic numbers of the target. Additionally, the impact of laser intensity and the number of electrons in the target on these production rates is investigated.

Event detection involves identifying the onset of specific occurrences within a time series. This study introduces a novel approach to event detection that utilizes a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) alongside a new method for calculating syntactic importance scores. The study also details a gate diversity mechanism designed to enhance the effectiveness of the GCN. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques across various event detection tasks.

This paper establishes geometric ergodicity for Gibbs samplers within Bayesian error-in-variable regression models, covering both normal and t-distributed errors. We demonstrate that, barring specific exceptions, the Gibbs sampler exhibits ergodicity in the geometry of the sum of squares of the regressors and the standard deviations of these errors. In the context of normal errors, we prove that geometric ergodicity holds even when the regressor vector is collinear with a specified direction provided it possesses at least one non-zero element. These findings are supported by numerical simulations and extend upon earlier work by Best and Sugden (1990) and Rosenthal (1991), which focused on linear regression with normal errors, as well as by Best and Sugden (1990) and Rosenthal (1990), which addressed normal error-in-variable regression.

This study examines the robust control of quantum sensors within the framework of multi-qubit systems subject to unknown environmental interactions. We introduce a new robust optimal control strategy that integrates the advantages of model predictive control with the certainty equivalence principle. This approach utilizes a Markov decision process to identify the most favorable control sequence for a specified time window, while the certainty equivalence principle determines initial control values by solving a simplified optimization problem derived from an idealized, non-interacting system model. Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the model predictive control approach alone.

This study examines the propagation of waves within scattering media characterized by nonlinear absorption. We develop a framework for deriving a corresponding nonlinear transport equation, which is subsequently analyzed for its well-posedness. Furthermore, a numerical scheme is formulated to address this transport equation, and numerical experiments are conducted to assess its performance.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved remarkable success in numerous domains, including game playing, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, the "black box" nature of these models has generated significant concern regarding their reliability and interpretability. To address this, researchers have developed explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) to enhance model transparency. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of XRL methods, examining their origins, underlying techniques, and specific applications. Furthermore, the study highlights existing challenges and future research directions within the field.

This work examines one-variable logics grounded in algebras featuring a single operation, focusing on a class where the operation is a lattice homomorphism that is either a projection or a specific type of image. We introduce a novel algebraic framework, known as the algebraic semantics for these logics, which serves as a bridge between these one-variable structures and their corresponding lattice-valuated counterparts. We demonstrate that this new semantic system is sound and complete for the logic, and we establish that it constitutes a pseudovariety.

This paper investigates the Wiener chaos expansion of both the random multiple iterated integrals and the signature associated with a Gaussian process. By imposing specific constraints on the reproducing kernel Hilbert space underlying the process, we investigate the corresponding Wiener chaos expansions. We demonstrate that if the covariance function's mixed partial derivatives of order $2d$ are square-integrable over $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$, then the $d$-th chaos component of this expansion can be explicitly formulated using mixed multiple iterated integrals. Furthermore, by summing these chaos components across all $d$, we derive an explicit expression for the Fourier–Walsh series of the signature.

Millimeter-wave (mmWave) cellular networks are anticipated to be pivotal for fifth-generation (5G) and subsequent generations of wireless systems. Although mmWave signals are highly directional, which theoretically enhances localization precision, the accuracy of such processes is significantly influenced by the stochastic nature of the network's spatial layout. This paper investigates the performance of user localization within a mmWave cellular environment by examining the statistical characteristics of the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) for position estimation. Specifically, we derive a closed-form approximation for the CRLB of the x-coordinate in a two-dimensional space, accounting for both horizontal and vertical components of the mmWave signal. Furthermore, we analyze the CRLB's statistical properties, including its mean and variance, to evaluate how network parameters affect localization outcomes. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed analytical framework accurately characterizes the CRLB, thereby offering a robust method for assessing localization efficiency in mmWave cellular infrastructures.

We demonstrate the existence of a Bose-Einstein condensate in trapped systems using the energy method applied to Gross-Pitaevskii energy functionals. This approach extends previous findings by Esteban, Séré, and Sierakowski, which were established for free space, by addressing the challenges posed by the trapped energy functional.

Image inpainting involves reconstructing missing or corrupted image regions. Although deep learning has significantly advanced this field, most current methods struggle with high-resolution images, often requiring prohibitively long training times. To address this, we introduce a two-stage deep learning framework designed to enhance inpainting performance on high-resolution imagery. The initial stage employs a two-stage architecture to generate a coarse inpainting result, which is then refined in the second stage by integrating both the original image and the preliminary output to produce the final high-resolution restoration. This approach is evaluated on the CelebA dataset, where it achieves a state-of-the-art PSNR of 29.17 and an SSIM of 0.822.

This study examines stochastic bandit scenarios characterized by structured reward distributions. We introduce a novel perspective wherein the reward function is modeled as a sum comprising a structured mean component and stochastic noise. We demonstrate that the regret lower bound varies significantly based on the specific distribution of this noise. Specifically, we analyze two distinct distributions: the uniform distribution and the Bernoulli distribution. For the Bernoulli case, our derived lower bound surpasses the current best-known bound by a factor of $\sqrt{\frac{K}{2}}$.

This paper presents an exponential compression of the proof system originally described in NP vs PSPACE [GKR18], specifically targeting the verification of refutations for the pigeonhole relation via the combination of circuit lower bounds and the RRA proof system. The compressed proofs have a size scaling of $O(\log n \cdot \log \log n \cdot \text{poly}(n))$, which represents a significant improvement over the original $O(n^2)$ bound. This result is achieved by adapting the technique from [GKR18] that utilized the circuit size lower bounds of Ajtai and Furst-Sipser to verify circuit size constraints. The authors demonstrate that the same lower bounds can be leveraged to verify the circuit size constraints within the compressed proof structure.

This paper demonstrates the existence of solutions to $H^\alpha$-flow for mean convex, complete graphical hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, where $\alpha \geq 1$, by utilizing the heat equation with an additional potential term.

We derive exact sum rules governing vortex-pair fluctuations within a Coulomb gas model of a 2D superfluid. These rules connect the second virial coefficient to the superfluid fraction, the superfluid's compressibility, and the total energy of an infinite vortex lattice.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming our world, yet we lack empirical data on how the general public perceives it. To address this, we conducted a survey of 10,000 participants across eight nations, examining their knowledge of AI, their attitudes toward it, and their expectations for its future. Our findings reveal that while 60% of respondents possess a basic understanding of AI, the majority hold positive views of it. Furthermore, respondents anticipate that AI will have a significant impact on their daily lives. These conclusions are robust across diverse demographic groups, including gender, age, and education levels.

The suppressed decay $\Xi_c^0\to \pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ has been observed for the first time with a measured branching fraction of $(1.0\pm0.3\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$. This result is based on an analysis of $1.36$ fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV by the LHCb detector.

This study aims to investigate the fixed point behavior of the composite product of two nonlinear operators within Banach algebras. We establish several new convergence theorems regarding such products, relying on notions of joint spectral radius and operator products. Furthermore, we provide illustrative examples to support our findings and demonstrate how these methods can be applied to analyze the solvability of specific non-linear integral equations.

Actor-Critic (AC) reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for solving complex tasks. However, the performance of AC algorithms is often hindered by the high variance inherent in the critic's estimation of the policy's value. This study introduces a novel AC framework that integrates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to reduce this variance. By leveraging the critic's ability to estimate the energy function, the proposed method guides HMC sampling to generate more accurate estimates of the policy's value. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can be implemented using a single critic, which enhances its efficiency. Experimental results across multiple tasks indicate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art AC methods.

We investigate the Dicke model, a paradigmatic example of superradiance, within a triangular optical cavity setup. By analyzing the system's phase diagram, we demonstrate that the interplay between cavity geometry and atom-light coupling can induce a quantum tricritical point. This tricritical point serves as the convergence location for two distinct quantum phase transitions, each characterized by a diverging order parameter. Furthermore, we observe that the nature of tricriticality is not uniform across the diagram; instead, it varies with the coupling strength, shifting between Z_2 and Z_3 symmetry types.

Although transfer learning has proven highly effective in single-agent reinforcement learning, its application to multi-agent scenarios remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces a novel cooperative multi-agent transfer learning framework designed to leverage knowledge from a source domain to accelerate learning in a target domain. Central to our approach is a level-adaptive credit assignment mechanism that evaluates the value of source state-action pairs based on the transferability of underlying skills. This is achieved by estimating the value of target-domain counterparts for source components and comparing them against the actual achieved values. Consequently, this method enables the system to selectively discard non-transferable or suboptimal source information, thereby enhancing the robustness of the transfer learning process. Experimental results across three cooperative multi-agent tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both transfer accuracy and computational efficiency.

This paper introduces a novel simulator designed to facilitate the development and assessment of deep reinforcement learning strategies for particle-based robots. We have engineered a versatile environment capable of modeling particle robots composed of both repulsive and attractive particles, alongside various object types. To demonstrate the platform's utility, we applied it to two representative challenges: navigating particle robots through mazes and relocating objects. Our results indicate that Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) excels in maze navigation, whereas a neural network trained via Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) proves more effective for object manipulation.

We report the detection of a 3-sigma absence of potassium in the atmosphere of WASP-31b, based on a novel, high-resolution transmission spectrum obtained via the Keck/MIKE instrument. This finding is significant because it contradicts earlier low-resolution studies that suggested potassium absorption. The high spectral resolution achieved here allows for the precise identification of telluric lines, thereby eliminating a potential source of error in spectral analysis. The resulting spectrum reveals no evidence of potassium absorption at the 3-sigma level, with an upper limit on the abundance of $< 10^{6.5}$ (relative to hydrogen). This constraint is consistent with prior observations of sodium and magnesium, suggesting that potassium may be depleted by a factor of 1000 relative to solar abundance. The absence of potassium is likely attributable to the planet's proximity to the host star, which drives the rapid photodissociation of K into atomic forms that are subsequently lost to space.

Cloud-based High-Performance Computing-as-a-Service (HPCaaS) is rapidly gaining traction, yet it currently faces significant hurdles, primarily stemming from the necessity of reinitializing applications and transferring datasets upon rescheduling. This research introduces a novel, secure, and cost-effective architecture designed to eliminate these inefficiencies by leveraging Non-Volatile RAM (NVRAM). The proposed solution employs a virtualized, distributed NVRAM infrastructure that ensures data persistence across virtual machines, enabling the resumption of tasks from their exact points of suspension. Furthermore, this architecture facilitates data sharing among virtual machines and allows for the reuse of pre-warmed compute resources. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated through a proof-of-concept implementation and an evaluation using a realistic HPC workload. The findings indicate that this architecture can cut application resumption and data transfer durations by 99.5% and 99.3%, respectively.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a non-invasive neuroimaging technique that maps brain activity to specific cognitive or behavioral tasks. While the field has seen significant progress in applying deep learning to fMRI data for population-level classification, such as diagnosing neurological disorders, these methods often struggle with the modality's inherent challenges: high dimensionality, low signal-to-noise ratios, and substantial inter-individual variability. To address these issues, we introduce a novel contrastive graph learning framework designed to enhance population fMRI classification. Our approach leverages graph neural networks to capture inter-subject relationships, while simultaneously employing contrastive learning to refine the learned representations. Specifically, we utilize the contrastive mechanism to suppress noise and isolate task-related signals, thereby increasing the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, we apply contrastive learning to the graph itself to mitigate inter-subject variability, ensuring that the model focuses on task-specific features rather than individual differences. Extensive experiments on fMRI datasets from the Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) challenges demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper explores Gauss sums, beginning with their historical origins and initial investigations into properties before delving into their modern applications. The discussion covers finite fields, Dirichlet characters, and their connection to class numbers, alongside their role in topology where they appear in the form of twisted quantum mechanical systems. The text examines the relationship between these Gauss sums and the properties of twisted quantum mechanical systems in topology, concluding with an overview of their significance in number theory and physics.

Cherenkov radiation is a well-known phenomenon that occurs when a charged particle travels through a dielectric medium at a speed exceeding the medium's phase velocity of light. While this effect is widely documented in optical and infrared domains, it has historically been elusive in the X-ray spectrum due to its extremely short wavelength. This study presents the first experimental detection of Cherenkov radiation in the soft X-ray band, generated by 1.17 MeV electrons passing through thin beryllium and silicon foils. The observed spectral distribution aligns with theoretical predictions, confirming the presence of the phenomenon in this previously inaccessible frequency range.

The Unconditional Construction Algorithm (UCCA) offers a robust framework for modeling semantic relationships among clauses, including those involving implicit arguments. This work details a novel approach to identifying and labeling these arguments within the UCCA schema, utilizing user feedback to refine the outputs of a machine learning model. We present results from two distinct user studies: the first evaluates the performance of various machine learning configurations, while the second assesses user proficiency in annotating implicit arguments and refining UCCA graphs. Our findings indicate that incorporating human feedback substantially enhances annotation quality, with users achieving an accuracy of 85% in identifying and labeling implicit arguments.

Weakly supervised disease localization in chest radiographs is a critical yet difficult task, primarily because standard training datasets only provide image-level labels rather than precise bounding boxes. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework designed for weakly supervised disease detection and localization. Our approach leverages a self-guided training strategy that utilizes the model's own predictions to refine localization accuracy. Specifically, we employ a two-stage process: first, a weakly supervised model generates initial bounding box estimates; second, a MIL-based model trains using these predictions as pseudo ground truth. To further enhance performance, we incorporate several auxiliary losses and propose a new attention-based instance selection strategy. Extensive experiments on the CheXpert dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches in both disease classification and localization accuracy.

We introduce a new model selection strategy grounded in the minimum penalized Hellinger distance, specifically designed to handle the challenges of small sample sizes and high dimensionality. This approach is evaluated through a simulation study, where it is shown to outperform the standard AIC and BIC criteria. Furthermore, the method is applied to a contemporary study of the expanding universe involving data from the Pantheon supernova dataset.

We investigate the distribution of binary word occurrences within the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence. While the number of first-order occurrences remains balanced between the two symbols, the counts of longer words diverge. We establish that the count of a specific word differs from its bitwise negation by a magnitude no greater than half its length in binary representation. This bound is asymptotically optimal, and the proof leverages a novel combinatorial method. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a direct link between the counting function for these words and the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence itself.

This study introduces a new approach to dynamic classifier selection tailored for multi-class problems. The method leverages hierarchical clustering to identify optimal subsets of classifiers for each target class, subsequently employing a cost-sensitive variant of the nearest neighbor algorithm to determine the final selection for every class. This novel strategy is evaluated against the contemporary $k$-Best Subsets of Classifiers (k-BSC) method, which applies the same clustering technique but utilizes the 1-Nearest Neighbor classifier instead. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms k-BSC in terms of classification accuracy.

The Tianlai project is a low-frequency radio telescope initiative designed to investigate the early universe. Its 128-channel system, comprising 16 8-element arrays, operates across the 80–400 MHz frequency range. This study outlines the data processing pipeline for Tianlai, which facilitates the extraction of scientific data from raw telescope recordings. The workflow includes data calibration, filtering, and the computation of power spectra. Additionally, we present preliminary findings regarding the power spectra of the cosmic microwave background and the 21-cm signal from the epoch of reionization.

We investigate the magnetic characteristics of the monolayer materials VSi2P4, VSi2N4, and NbSi2N4. Our findings indicate that these monolayers exhibit robust ferromagnetism, with NbSi2N4 and VSi2P4 displaying the highest saturation magnetization of 10.0 and 10.1 μB per unit cell, respectively. Additionally, we calculated the Curie temperature ($T_C$) for these materials, observing that NbSi2N4 and VSi2P4 possess $T_C$ values of 300 K and 350 K, respectively, suggesting their potential utility in spintronic applications.

Gneiting's approach to positively definite functions on Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^d$ spaces relies on two core principles: the spectral representation of such functions and their characterization via Fourier transforms. This paper extends that methodology to metric space domains. Our proposed technique is both flexible and intuitive, allowing for the creation of new functions that are not merely extensions of existing forms found in literature, but novel constructions.

A positive monoid $\mathcal{M}$ is defined as atomic when its elements decompose into irreducible components in a unique way, with respect to a unique factorization property. This paper establishes that every finite positive monoid possesses this atomic nature. The argument relies on the fact that any finite positive monoid $\mathcal{M}$ can be represented as a submonoid of a specific free monoid formed by the irreducible elements of $\mathcal{M}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any positive monoid derived from the context of Petri nets is atomic. This finding extends a previous result by L. Comon, who established the same property for monoids consisting solely of permutations.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (AFme) quantifies the reduction in disease incidence that would occur if all exposed individuals were hypothetically removed from the population. While this metric is crucial for evaluating causal impacts of exposures, its estimation typically relies on data from observational studies, which are often subject to selection bias. This bias can severely distort AFme values, leading to incorrect conclusions regarding the causal benefits of an exposure. This paper introduces a novel semiparametric estimator for AFme that utilizes covariate information detailing the specific reasons individuals selected into the study. By integrating these case description details, the estimator effectively mitigates selection bias, thereby enhancing the accuracy of causal effect measurement.

This article investigates zero-cycles on normal projective varieties situated over an algebraically closed field, specifically examining those with a canonical singularities. We demonstrate that such varieties satisfy the property of rational homological triviality. Furthermore, we provide a counterexample showing that they do not necessarily meet the condition of being numerically trivial.

The analysis utilizes data from the CMS detector, which was collected during 2010 with the LHC operating at this energy. The $\Upsilon$(nS) mesons are identified through their decay into a pair of muons. Quantum dot systems are highly promising for quantum information processing, yet their strong coupling to the environment often leads to decoherence, which hinders their utility. While entropy serves as a vital metric for characterizing quantum systems, measuring it in quantum dots has remained challenging. This study demonstrates that quantum entropy can be determined by analyzing the heat capacity of a quantum dot, a method that is both simple and effective. This approach is applied to investigate the strongly coupled dynamics of a double quantum dot system, specifically examining how the heat-bath temperature influences the entropy of the quantum dot and the resulting impact on the heat capacity.

This work introduces a new principle, extending the Geometric Modulus Principle to encompass both holomorphic and harmonic functions. Furthermore, we utilize this principle to derive the Geometric Maximum Modulus Principle as a direct corollary.

This study investigates the stability of discrete solitons within a 1D nonpolynomial Schrödinger equation (NDSE) featuring dipole-dipole interactions. Our analysis reveals that these NDSE solitons exhibit a stability profile comparable to that of the standard discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation (DNSE), with a notable exception: the presence of long-range interactions in the NDSE allows for soliton collapse. Specifically, we identify a critical radius beyond which the soliton becomes unstable. This critical threshold is determined by the interaction strength and the lattice coupling constant.

Signomial programming (SP) is defined as an optimization task where the objective function and constraints consist of sums of non-negative terms, each represented by a product of variables raised to real-valued powers. This class of functions is not closed under standard operations such as addition or multiplication. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm based on the majorization-minimization (MM) framework, which iteratively minimizes a majorizing surrogate function that approximates the original objective. By leveraging the algebraic characteristics of signomials, we construct this surrogate function as a combination of geometric means. Consequently, the subsequent subproblem reduces to solving a geometric programming (GP) task, for which efficient solution techniques are well-established. We demonstrate that this proposed method converges to a stationary point of the original problem. Furthermore, we examine the algorithm's performance on SP instances, comparing it against existing approaches.

Teichmuller spaces serve as moduli spaces that parameterize Riemann surfaces, with their associated Jacobians representing the corresponding moduli spaces of Abelian varieties. This paper explores the Teichmuller map, which maps these spaces from Riemann surfaces to their corresponding Abelian varieties. This mapping is known to be an embedding when restricted to the interior of the Witten-Weissman polytope, a result established by the authors. Furthermore, the authors present a novel proof of the global Torelli theorem for Abelian varieties, demonstrating that this map is surjective for any Riemann surface, provided the Jacobian is simple. This proof relies on the study of the cohomology of the moduli space of pairs consisting of a curve with its associated linear system.

Our method utilizes a 2.5D representation derived from this input to train a network that predicts the appearance of a specific individual across various virtual camera angles. This architecture is trained on a large-scale, multi-person dataset to learn a universal prior for human appearance, which is then adapted to the target subject using the recorded footage. This study introduces a new method for facial de-occlusion that leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct occluded facial regions. The approach utilizes a 3D face model to synthesize a 2D latent representation, which is then processed by the GAN to generate the restored face. To address the challenge of limited training data, we developed a data augmentation strategy that expands the available dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques, particularly in scenarios involving hair occlusion.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in various fields, including robotics, gaming, and autonomous driving. However, current RL methods face a critical limitation: they necessitate external human intervention to supply reward signals, which is often unavailable in real-world scenarios. This dependency hinders the deployment of RL in practical applications. To address this, researchers have introduced autonomous RL (ARL), which empowers agents to learn without external assistance by generating their own intrinsic rewards. This approach enables agents to autonomously identify and pursue tasks based on their inherent curiosity. This paper provides a concise overview of ARL, covering its fundamental concepts, key algorithms, and promising application areas.

This work introduces a Localized Policy Iteration (LPI) algorithm designed for decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning (MRL) within networked environments. Unlike traditional centralized approaches that rely on a global MDP model, LPI operates without such global knowledge, relying instead on a decentralized architecture to facilitate agent-to-agent communication. We demonstrate that LPI achieves global convergence to the optimal Q-function for both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes. Furthermore, we establish that LPI exhibits linear convergence rates for both MDP types, provided the communication network is sufficiently dense. The algorithm's efficacy is validated through numerical experiments on a networked MDP.

This study examines dijet events characterized by a large rapidity gap separating the two leading jets. The analysis utilizes a jet-finding algorithm that identifies the two highest transverse momentum jets, $p_{\rm T}^{\rm jet} > 20$ GeV, and a leading jet with $p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{leading}} > 200$ GeV. The dataset comprises 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV by the CMS detector at the LHC. The observed production cross section for these events is measured at 0.13 pb, with a statistical uncertainty of 10% and a systematic uncertainty of 20%. Additionally, the study presents the distribution of the rapidity gap between the two jets and compares these findings with theoretical predictions from the PYTHIA and HERWIG Monte Carlo simulations.

Two-dimensional materials have recently emerged as a promising avenue for thermoelectric applications. This study investigates the thermoelectric properties of penta-silicene, a newly discovered 2D material. Our findings indicate that penta-silicene exhibits an exceptionally high Seebeck coefficient of 110 mV/K at room temperature, driven by its unique electronic band structure characterized by a local peak near the Fermi level. Furthermore, the material's low lattice thermal conductivity, resulting from its complex phonon dispersion, facilitates a high figure of merit (ZT) of 0.11 at room temperature. These results suggest that penta-silicene is a highly effective thermoelectric candidate.

This study examines the influence of a strong external magnetic field on the mass spectra of heavy quarkonia ($J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$, $\psi(2S)$, $\Upsilon(1S)$) within a hot environment. We employ a fractional non-relativistic quantum mechanical framework to analyze the system, utilizing the Cornell potential augmented by a linear magnetic term. The analysis incorporates a temperature-dependent modification to the string tension, $\sigma(T)$, which is determined using the pQCD-based perturbative method. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field significantly alters the mass spectra of the heavy quarkonia, a result that aligns with calculations based on the finite-temperature Dirac equation.

This study examines the potential for dark matter (DM) detection in subhalos via scattering interactions, specifically focusing on neutron stars, cosmic rays, and ancient meteorites. We establish the necessary conditions for DM to be captured by these subhalos and subsequently detected through scattering. Our analysis reveals that DM-neutron star interactions can be probed by observing the gravitational wave signals from binary mergers, while cosmic ray detection is feasible through the observation of secondary DM decay products. Additionally, we demonstrate that DM can be identified by analyzing neutron capture gamma rays in meteorites, provided the DM interacts with neutrons. We further quantify the expected signal strengths for each detection method and outline the necessary parameters for observing DM signals in these three scenarios.

This study examines a signaling game involving a pursuer and evaders, where the pursuer must simultaneously decide on allocation and patrolling strategies under conditions of uncertainty. The pursuer's uncertainty stems from two factors: the unknown number of evaders and their unobservable locations. The objective for the pursuer is to minimize the expected time required to capture an evader. To address this challenge, we introduce a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework that jointly optimizes allocation and patrolling. The core of this approach is a novel signaling game algorithm that dynamically selects the most probable node for evader presence based on a Bayesian inference process. The efficacy of this method is validated through extensive simulations.

This paper introduces a new approach for autonomous robot planning within uncertain outdoor settings, specifically targeting the challenge of navigating uneven terrains. We present a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework that learns a policy for robot locomotion by utilizing a suite of depth sensors. This method is designed to be robust against depth data inaccuracies and sensor failures, enabling reliable operation in unknown outdoor environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly enhances the success rate of robot navigation in such settings. Furthermore, we validate the method through a real-world testbed using a robot equipped with a depth camera, confirming its effectiveness in executing complex maneuvers on unpredictable outdoor landscapes.

We examine the stability of axially symmetric magnetic fields within a slowly rotating star, specifically addressing the $Z$-component ($B_z$) and the azimuthal component ($B_\phi$). Our analysis demonstrates that the $B_z$ component is inherently stable. Conversely, the $B_\phi$ field exhibits stability only if it is co-rotated with the star; if it rotates against the stellar spin, it becomes unstable. This instability arises from the torquing effect of the magnetic field on the star, which can exceed the energy dissipation caused by viscosity.

Simplicial synchronization represents a novel framework for coordinating networks that includes not only pairwise interactions but also higher-order relationships. This study examines the topological and geometric characteristics of the synchrony patterns generated by simplicial coupling. We establish that the network's global synchronization state is contingent upon the interplay between its underlying graph topology and the specific simplicial coupling structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stability of the resulting synchronized state relies on the curvature defined by the geometric arrangement of the network's nodes.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) serves as a foundational operation within numerous iterative linear solvers, making it a critical component of scientific computing. This study examines SpMV performance across diverse architectures, including CPUs, GPUs, and GPUs, while also assessing its impact on iterative solvers. We evaluate both CPU and GPU implementations, analyzing how specific optimization strategies affect SpMV and iterative solver performance. Our findings indicate that while these strategies can significantly boost SpMV efficiency, they do not always lead to corresponding improvements in solver convergence.

This paper examines the normality of one family of meromorphic functions relative to another, utilizing the concept of shared value evaluation. Let $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ denote two families of meromorphic functions defined on the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. A family $\mathcal{F}$ is considered $\sigma$-normal with respect to another family $\mathcal{M}$ if, for every $\sigma\in\mathcal{M}$, the collection $\mathcal{F}_\sigma=\{\frac{f'}{(f-\sigma)}:f\in\mathcal{M}\}$ is normal in $\mathbb{C}$. In this context, we explore the $\sigma$-normality of $\mathcal{F}$ relative to $\mathcal{M}$ by analyzing the properties of the associated family $\mathcal{F}_\sigma$.

Human collaboration with robots is often hindered by a lack of mutual understanding of intentions. While current methods for recognizing these intentions typically depend on wearable eye-tracking devices, their reliance on bulky equipment and the need for line-of-sight restricts their practicality. To address this limitation, we introduce HAIR, a novel intention recognition system designed for use with head-mounted displays. By utilizing AR glasses, HAIR captures both visual data and physiological signals, such as pupil dilation, to identify intentions. We validated HAIR through a human-robot interaction experiment involving a human, a robot, and a machine learning algorithm. The results demonstrate that HAIR can accurately detect intentions with 90% precision. Furthermore, the system exhibits robustness against movement and maintains a low latency of 16 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-time applications.

Monge-Amp\`ere systems are characterized by the property that their covariant forms are closed. This study introduces a new category of such systems, termed "Monge-Amp\`ere systems with Lagrangian pairs," which are distinguished by the fact that their covariant forms are not closed but instead satisfy the Poisson bracket equal to zero. This work establishes the correspondence between these systems and nonholonomic integrable systems, and it demonstrates that their associated covariant forms can be expressed as exact differentials of specific functionals.

This study examines the impact of buoyancy-driven convection on the nucleation and growth of bubbles at an electrode submerged in an electrolyte. The analysis begins with a steady-state, laminar flow regime where the fluid is stationary, and the bubble growth rate is governed by diffusion. Subsequently, the model incorporates the effects of convection, which accelerates mass transport and alters the growth dynamics. The results indicate that convection significantly influences bubble formation, with the onset of convective effects occurring when the Rayleigh number exceeds a critical threshold. As the Rayleigh number increases, the transition from diffusion-dominated to convection-controlled mass transport occurs at progressively smaller bubble sizes. Furthermore, the study reveals that convective effects can lead to the dissolution of bubbles, particularly in scenarios where the solute concentration within the bubble is lower than that of the bulk fluid.

This study reports a search for long-lived particles (LLPs) in proton-proton collisions at the CMS detector within the LHC's 13 TeV dataset, collected in 2016 with an integrated luminosity of 35.6 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on a signature involving a displaced photon vertex originating from a LLP decay, accompanied by a high-transverse-momentum photon. The results indicate no significant excess beyond the expected background, leading to the establishment of exclusion limits for a 100 GeV c\textasciitilde{}charged scalar particle with a lifetime of 100 ps. These findings constrain the parameter space of the scalar leptoquark model and the little Higgs model with extra U(1) symmetry.

We introduce a correlated second-order Dirac semimetal (SO DSM) characterized by a unique Fermi surface where the correlated band structure features a four-fold degenerate point. This system is realized in a $d$-wave Mott insulator with a square lattice, where the correlated band structure is tuned by the bare hopping amplitude. The SO DSM is defined by a four-fold degenerate saddle point at the $\Gamma$ point and a second such point at the $(\pi,0)$ position. We demonstrate that the saddle point at the $\Gamma$ point is unstable, leading to a correlated Fermi liquid phase. Furthermore, we analyze the phase diagram of the SO DSM, identifying a superconducting phase that emerges from the instability at the $\Gamma$ point. This superconducting phase is characterized by a $d$-wave gap, with the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) increasing as the instability at the $\Gamma$ point intensifies.

This paper introduces a new program synthesis approach designed to automatically create concurrent implementations of abstract data structures. The method utilizes program transformations grounded in logical reasoning about the sequential behavior and invariants of these data structures to derive concurrent variants. By employing answer set programming, we encode synthesis rules and data structure invariants as logical constraints. The resulting programs are verified through a two-stage process: first, we use linear temporal logic to confirm that the implementation satisfies sequential invariants, and second, we apply a model checker to validate that specific invariants are upheld within each data structure.

We introduce a novel experimental approach to test fundamental physics by utilizing a low-temperature, low-dissipation, and high-quality magnetically levitated resonator. This system allows for the precise measurement of minute inertial forces, offering a powerful means to investigate potential deviations from standard physical laws. We demonstrate that such a setup can detect modifications to gravity, specifically by identifying deviations from the inverse-square law of Newtonian gravity.

We report the detection of two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) in the TMC-1 dark cloud: the 1,2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopadiene (1,2-EPDC) and 1,3-ethynyl-1,4-cyclopadiene (1,3-1,4-EPDC). These findings are based on observations made with the IRAM 30-m telescope, where we identified 13 and 12 transitions, respectively, for both species. The derived column densities are $1.2 \times 10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$ for 1,2-EPDC and $1.0 \times 10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$ for 1,3-1,4-EPDC. These values represent the first detection of any ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomer and the first observation of a 1,3-1,4-EPDC isomer. The abundance ratio between 1,2-EPDC and 1,3-1,4-EPDC is approximately 1.2, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we report the first detection of the cyanogen (CN) derivative of cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH), specifically the 1,3-1

We investigate asymmetric dark matter scenarios where the asymmetry between dark matter and its antiparticle originates from decays of heavy particles. These decays generate both a baryon asymmetry and a dark matter asymmetry by producing both particles and their antiparticles in unequal amounts. The resulting asymmetry in dark matter density is established through the suppression of annihilation processes by the existing asymmetry, while the residual annihilation cross-section determines the observed dark matter density via thermal freeze-out. We demonstrate that the stochastic gravitational wave background emitted during the freeze-out epoch can provide a direct probe of this dark matter annihilation cross-section.

This study presents measurements of top-quark pair production alongside a Z boson in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on events containing two opposite-sign, same-flavor leptons (electrons or muons) and at least one additional isolated lepton of the same flavor. The measured fiducial cross-sections for the Z boson decaying to leptons are determined to be 1.00 ± 0.07 (stat.) ± 0.03 (syst.) pb for electrons and 0.77 ± 0.05 (stat.) ± 0.03 (syst.) pb for muons. These results align well with Standard Model predictions. Additionally, differential cross-sections are evaluated across various final-state kinematic variables, including the Z boson transverse momentum, the number of jets, and the invariant mass of the lepton pair.

We present a classification of single-time sections of the trajectory of a four-rebit quantum system, where a rebit is defined as a quantum entity restricted to real Hilbert spaces. This system serves as a precursor to the well-established trajectory of a four-qubit quantum system. We identify a total of 121 distinct equivalence classes of endpoint states under unitary equivalence, which are invariant under dynamical evolution. This categorization is achieved by applying a specific group of local transformations that leave the trajectory invariant, utilizing the theory of invariants and the theory of orbits.

Predictive State Representations (PSRs) offer an alternative to traditional Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by defining a system through observable states, prediction capabilities, and a reward function. Unlike standard MDP formulations, PSRs do not explicitly model underlying physical states, thereby circumventing issues related to partial observability. However, the original PSR reward mechanism is limited to exogenous rewards, which are independent of an agent's actions. This paper introduces a new class of rewards that integrates both exogenous and endogenous components, allowing for the representation of rewards that depend on an agent's behavior. We demonstrate that this expanded reward structure maintains PSR core properties, including finite representability and a well-defined belief state. Furthermore, we provide a novel formulation of the PSR value function that unifies both reward types and define a corresponding class of optimal policies.

Gentrification is a complex, multi-faceted process that is difficult to track and analyze. This study introduces a new early warning system designed to monitor gentrification in Buffalo, New York, utilizing a unique dataset of 100,000 real estate transactions. The approach employs a novel methodology for calculating gentrification indices and applies machine learning to forecast future development trends. The results indicate that this system effectively identifies areas undergoing gentrification and predicts future changes with an 80% accuracy rate. Furthermore, the study highlights the critical role of data granularity in comprehending the nuances of gentrification.

Chiral magnets are renowned for their diverse magnetic textures, including skyrmions, which are topologically protected spin textures. While these skyrmions are typically stable at low temperatures, they can undergo a "topological melting" into a skyrmion lattice as thermal energy increases. This study utilizes magnetic force microscopy to investigate the thermal evolution of skyrmions in the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$. The researchers observed that the skyrmion lattice melts into a uniform magnetic state at a temperature of 100 K. Furthermore, they noted that the skyrmion lattice exhibits a metastable state, persisting up to 150 K before topological melting occurs. The metastability of the skyrmion lattice is attributed to the competition between the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and the magnetostatic interaction.

This paper investigates composition operators within harmonic Bloch-type spaces by determining their respective ranks and determinants. Additionally, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a composition operator on these spaces to be compact, compact in the sense of norm, or strictly compact.

The widespread adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is a critical step toward achieving carbon neutrality. However, the limited energy storage capacity of current EV batteries and the insufficient coverage of charging infrastructure remain significant obstacles to their mass deployment. To address these challenges, this study introduces a range-extended electric vehicle (REEV) model that utilizes a generator to recharge the battery, thereby mitigating infrastructure constraints. We propose a joint routing framework that simultaneously optimizes the movement of REEVs and conventional vehicles across a metropolitan network. This approach employs a graph-based representation to model the region, where nodes signify locations like intersections or parking lots, and edges represent the connections between them. We develop a joint routing algorithm that determines optimal paths for both vehicle types, aiming to minimize total travel costs. This algorithm is validated using a real-world dataset from the Greater Toronto Area, demonstrating its effectiveness in large-scale urban environments.

This study examines the distribution amplitudes of heavy mesons and quarkonia within the light-front framework. We analyze the leading-twist distribution amplitudes for $D$ and $\eta_c$ mesons using the QCD sum rules method, considering both perturbative and non-perturbative contributions to the leading twist distribution amplitudes. Additionally, we explore the distribution amplitudes of heavy quarkonia in the context of the QCD factorization theorem.

This paper introduces a discrete-time framework for the analysis of a finite element method applied to transient problems. The study focuses on the enhanced velocity approach, which utilizes an approximation space for the displacement field that exceeds the smoothness requirements of classical Ciarard's theorem, a method known to yield superior a priori error estimates. The core of this analysis relies on a new error bound for the discrete-time finite element method, a bound that does not depend on the regularity of the exact solution. The methodology is applied to both the linear wave equation and the quasi-static biharmonic problem, achieving optimal convergence rates for the former and one additional order of convergence for the latter.

The growing adoption of autonomous vehicles necessitates a thorough understanding of the underlying technologies and the data models used to train them. This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing vision-based autonomous driving models by leveraging spatial video data. This approach incorporates a context-aware geospatial layer to facilitate the investigation of the relationship between these model outputs and the specific environments in which vehicles operate. The proposed methodology employs a multi-step process that includes data ingestion, data cleaning, and data enrichment. The framework is demonstrated using a real-world dataset comprising 10 million video frames from the OpenPilot dataset, which has been enhanced with spatial video data from OpenStreetMap.

This study examines the impact of illumination on photoionization within GaN MESFETs, specifically focusing on the effect of a parallel light source on the time-dependent behavior of trap occupancy. The results indicate that applying light from an additional source can enhance both the signal and the sensitivity of time-resolved measurements regarding trap population.

This paper introduces a particle filter framework designed to enhance Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) reliability by effectively handling multiple faults. The proposed method integrates two key components: a particle filter for localization and a particle filter-based fault detection and isolation (FDI) mechanism. The FDI system identifies faulty satellites and determines the specific nature of the fault by generating separate particles for each potential failure type. Subsequently, the localization system utilizes only the identified healthy satellites to compute accurate position estimates. The system's performance is evaluated through simulations involving various fault scenarios, including single satellite biases, multiple simultaneous faults, and a fault-free condition. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust localization performance across all tested scenarios.

We introduce SG-PALM, a novel algorithm designed to learn a sparse graphical model from tensor data. This approach is grounded in a proximal alternating linearized minimization framework, which ensures computational efficiency by utilizing closed-form solutions for updating model parameters. The resulting sparse graphical model offers a transparent interpretation of the tensor's underlying structure. Furthermore, we introduce a new sparsity metric tailored for tensors, which facilitates the application of SG-PALM to diverse tensor completion tasks. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that SG-PALM outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both speed and accuracy.

Counting fast-moving objects is a critical task in traffic management, yet it remains challenging for conventional cameras due to motion blur and missed detections. This study introduces an event camera-based approach utilizing a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to count rapid traffic flows. The method employs a 3D convolutional network to extract features from the raw asynchronous data stream, followed by a recurrent layer that aggregates these features to determine the final vehicle count. Evaluated on a real-world dataset, our approach achieves 98.7% accuracy and a mean absolute error of 0.48 vehicles per lane, outperforming existing event camera solutions that rely on traditional computer vision techniques.

This study investigates a heterogeneous network comprising a macro base station (MBS) and multiple small base stations (SBSs) that employ both network coding and multi-tier caching. The system architecture includes a two-tier cache structure: a lower tier located at the SBSs and an upper tier at the MBS. The paper addresses a throughput maximization problem by optimizing the SBS cache configuration, network coding parameters, and the association between users and base stations. To solve this, we propose a distributed algorithm that jointly optimizes these variables. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing schemes in terms of network throughput.
We demonstrate that any PPT matrix is impossible to constitute a perfect square of a positive definite matrix.

A Cayley graph $\Gamma$ is defined as normal edge-transitive if the group of automorphisms of $\Gamma$ that fix a designated vertex $u$ (denoted as $Aut(\Gamma)^{u}$) is a normal subgroup within the full automorphism group $Aut(\Gamma)$. This paper demonstrates that a finite Cayley graph $\Gamma$ possesses the normal edge-transitive property precisely when its connection group $G$ is generated by a subgroup $H$ that is normal in $Aut(\Gamma)^{u}$ and satisfies the condition $G = H \times \Gamma$.

This study introduces a new iterative approach to determine the optimal positions of range of arrival (TOA) anchors within a non-convex region located beyond the convex hull of target nodes. The primary objective is to minimize the maximum orthogonally projected residual distance (RNDOP) for all nodes, thereby establishing a conservative upper limit on the maximum possible localization error. The proposed iterative algorithm alternates between two steps: optimizing the projected distances for each node and subsequently updating the relative positions of the anchors. Theoretical analysis confirms that this algorithm converges to a local optimum. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

We examine the shear modulus within the atom-in-jellium framework, utilizing it as a theoretical model to describe neutral atoms confined in metallic environments. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to bulk materials, the shear modulus of these confined systems can vanish at a specific pressure threshold. We demonstrate that this phenomenon arises from the divergence of the Thomas-Fermi screening length and establish that the critical pressure marking this transition is inversely proportional to the square of the atomic radius.

This paper introduces a new approach to motion deblurring that leverages a deep neural network to create synthetic blur images from real sharp ones. The proposed method employs a two-stage pipeline: first, a neural network synthesizes a pseudo-blurred version of a real sharp image; subsequently, a dedicated deblurring network converts this synthetic blur back into a real sharp image. This framework is designed to address the scarcity of paired real-world sharp and blurred datasets. By generating synthetic data via the first stage, the system effectively trains a deblurring network to handle real-world scenarios. Our experiments on both real datasets and those generated by our own synthesizer demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are identified by a sudden rise in luminosity from a supermassive black hole (SMBH) that has engulfed a star. While the majority of TDEs are caused by SMBHs tearing apart stars, impostor events can arise from other phenomena, such as tidal disruption of brown dwarfs, stellar mergers, or tidal disruption of stellar-mass black holes. Distinguishing TDEs from impostors is crucial for understanding SMBH properties and their role in galaxy evolution. This study examines the feasibility of differentiating TDEs from impostors using the light curves of the most luminous events. We find that the light curves of brown dwarf TDEs and those caused by mergers or black hole collisions are indistinguishable from one another. However, brown dwarf TDEs and stellar mergers can be differentiated by the duration of the rising phase of the light curve. Furthermore, the light curves of black hole TDEs exhibit a significantly higher peak luminosity compared to those of brown dwarf TDEs. Consequently, the light curves of the most luminous TDEs can be classified into three categories: those from brown dwarf TDEs, those from mergers or brown dwarf TDEs, and those from black hole TDEs.

We have compiled a sample of 1,000 UV-bright Lyman $\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) from the Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey (CANDELS) to investigate the distribution of nearby galaxies. This study utilizes the $z$-band imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope to identify galaxies within 100 kpc of these LAs, classifying them as either star-forming or quiescent. Our results indicate that the fraction of star-forming galaxies in these environments is significantly higher than in the field, with the excess being more pronounced at smaller radii. Conversely, the fraction of quiescent galaxies remains consistent with the field average. These findings align with the "downsizing" paradigm, suggesting that star-forming galaxies are more prevalent in the early universe. Additionally, we observe that the stellar mass function of these galaxies is elevated compared to the field, with the most significant enhancement occurring at low stellar masses. This trend supports the notion that star-forming galaxies are the primary drivers of galaxy formation in the vicinity of LAEs.

We report new reflectance spectra of 10 cold classical trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) obtained using the Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). These objects are defined by their lack of significant scattering in their orbits, which suggests minimal collisional history since Neptune's migration. Our findings reveal that all 10 spectra exhibit a consistent, featureless, and highly reflective (approximately 80%) continuum across the 0.6 to 5.0 μm wavelength range. This uniformity indicates that cold classical TNOs share a common surface composition, likely dominated by a mixture of crystalline and amorphous ices. Notably, the spectra lack absorption features associated with methane ice, nitrogen ice, or organic compounds. These results imply that the volatile ices and organic materials typically found on other TNOs have been depleted from the cold classical population. This depletion likely occurred during the dynamical instabilities of the early solar system, which scattered these objects from the primordial Kuiper Belt disk.

Digital image correlation (DIC) was employed to examine the deformation of Ti$_6$Al alloy specimens during isothermal hold periods at 600°C, a condition that induces load shedding. The study reveals that the alloy experiences load shedding through a localized mechanism, where the load carried by a specific region diminishes as it undergoes plastic deformation. This process is driven by the localized formation of shear bands, which are accompanied by significant softening. Feature models serve as a graphical method for representing software product lines, defining the configurable options available to users. While numerous tools exist to visualize these models, their effectiveness in enhancing user comprehension remains uncertain. This study employed an eye-tracking experiment to compare the impact of different visualization techniques on the understanding of feature models. The research involved 24 participants tasked with answering questions about model content using either a tree-based or a dashboard-based visual representation. The findings indicate that dashboard-based visualizations lead to superior model comprehension. Furthermore, tree-based visuals draw a greater proportion of gaze fixations on mandatory elements compared to optional ones, a pattern not observed with dashboard-based visuals.

Close-in faint companions are vital for comprehending the evolution of binary systems and the formation of exoplanets. This study introduces StraKLIP, a novel pipeline that leverages the Karhunen-Loève Image Processing algorithm to identify and analyze such companions. The pipeline was tested on data from the 2.6m Nordic Optical Telescope, utilizing the NICS instrument, to search for companions around the bright star HD 168443. The analysis revealed a companion with a contrast of 1.2 magnitudes at a separation of 100 milliarcseconds. Spectral analysis of this companion yielded a spectral type of M6.5, a mass of 0.09 solar masses, and a radius of 0.13 solar radii. These findings suggest the object is a brown dwarf. The detection of this brown dwarf is significant because it is the closest one found to a solar-type star, representing the first such discovery using the NICS instrument.

We investigate the Page curve for the entanglement entropy of Hawking radiation within the Hayden-Preskill setup, specifically in a conformal field theory featuring a finite number of higher-form symmetries. Our findings indicate that the radiation's entanglement entropy adheres to the curve established by the Hayden-Preskill conjecture, which posits a rapid saturation of entropy at a threshold determined by the radiation's size. Specifically, we demonstrate that the radiation becomes decoupled from the initial state once it surpasses the higher-form symmetry charge threshold.

This study introduces a hierarchical, unsupervised framework designed for long-term video prediction. The approach leverages a hierarchical autoencoder to learn latent representations of video data, which are then utilized by a recurrent model to generate future frames. Empirical results indicate that this hierarchical architecture surpasses standard models in both accuracy and visual quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed hierarchical system is capable of predicting sequences lasting up to 100 frames.

Mitochondria are essential organelles responsible for cellular energy production and the regulation of cell death. Their population is dynamic, constantly shifting through fusion and fission processes that create interconnected networks. These networks are further modulated by mitochondrial dynamics genes (DMPs) and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). This study utilized a network-based approach to analyze how DMPs and mtDNA interact within mitochondrial systems. We developed a mathematical model that integrates DMPs and mtDNA to simulate network evolution, revealing that the structural state of the network significantly influences the dynamics of mtDNA. Specifically, our results indicate that a network's state can either amplify or suppress the impact of mtDNA dynamics. Furthermore, we identified that the network state is the primary factor governing the phenotypic consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction. Ultimately, these findings offer a novel framework for comprehending the phenotypic effects of mitochondrial disorders.

This study introduces Mixer-TTS, a non-autoregressive text-to-speech architecture that utilizes non-linear embeddings of text alongside acoustic conditioning. Mixer-TTS leverages the embedding of tokens from a pre-trained non-autoregressive text language model to facilitate the rapid generation of text sequences. The speech synthesis process is driven by a separate text language model, which operates independently of the speech model itself. This design enables the speech model to produce audio at speeds exceeding 1000 characters per second, while maintaining a significantly smaller parameter count than current state-of-the-art models. The authors demonstrate that Mixer-TTS achieves a balance of high efficiency and strong performance, with synthesis quality that rivals or exceeds that of autoregressive baselines.

Phase change materials (PCMs) are utilized in various applications, including optical storage, optical switching, and non-volatile memory. This study investigates the kinetics and mechanism of phase transitions in the fast-switching ternary alloy $Ge_2Sb_2Te_5$ (GST) by analyzing the temperature dependence of the refractive index ($n$) and extinction coefficient ($k$). The findings indicate that the crystallization process is a two-step event: the first step involves the segregation of Ge atoms from the SbTe matrix, while the second step entails the crystallization of the remaining SbTe phase. Furthermore, the optical bandgap ($E_g$) was determined to be 2.1 eV for the amorphous state and 1.6 eV for the crystalline state.

Topological insulators are a class of materials characterized by a topologically protected bulk state, which hosts robust, gapless, and chiral edge modes at the boundaries. While the Dirac cone found in two-dimensional (2D) topological insulators is typically isotropic, it can be distorted into an oblique form, resulting in a complex network of chiral edge modes. This study establishes a theoretical framework for oblique topological insulators, demonstrating that their edge structure is uniquely determined by the bulk topology. We further illustrate that the bulk-boundary correspondence remains valid for these systems, provided the bulk Hamiltonian is not Hermitian.

By utilizing a suite of hydrodynamical simulations, we examine the interplay between ice line shifts and the resulting variations in ice line positions. Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in various domains, including robotics, gaming, and autonomous driving. However, in real-world applications, data efficiency remains a critical challenge. This paper introduces the Contrastive-Curiosity-Driven Learning (CCLF) framework, which integrates contrastive learning with curiosity-driven RL to enhance sample efficiency. CCLF leverages contrastive learning to generate informative state representations, thereby strengthening the agent's ability to explore its environment. Furthermore, it employs curiosity-driven mechanisms to encourage exploration by rewarding novel states. We evaluate the CCLF framework across three distinct RL environments: the classic LunarLander, the CartPole balancing task, and the LunarLander variant. Experimental results demonstrate that CCLF surpasses existing baselines in both sample efficiency and final performance.

This study introduces a new dataset featuring 1,000 sentences across 14 Chinese dialects, designed to facilitate fine-grained dialect classification. We also present a hierarchical attention multi-task learning framework that leverages the BERT model to achieve state-of-the-art results on this task.

This paper addresses the two-dimensional strip packing challenge, specifically the task of arranging a set of rectangles into an infinitely high strip with minimum possible width. We introduce novel constant-factor approximation methods for a restricted variation known as a "guillotine" strip, where all resulting cuts are straight lines extending fully across the strip. We demonstrate that a straightforward greedy strategy yields a 4-approximation for a specific case, while a refined version of this approach achieves a 3.5-approximation for the general guillotine scenario. Furthermore, we establish that 4 and 5 are the tightest achievable approximation ratios for both scenarios.

We introduce a deep learning approach to estimate the masses of galaxy clusters using Comptonization ($Y$) parameters derived from the Planck satellite. Our method employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on simulated cluster data, where the input consists of the Comptonization map and the output is the cluster's virial mass. We demonstrate that this model achieves a median mass estimation accuracy of 10% for clusters with masses exceeding $10^{14} M_{\odot}$, a performance level comparable to that of the standard mass estimator, $M_{500}$. Additionally, we assess the model's robustness against various observational systematics, including instrumental noise, foreground contamination, and variations in the underlying cosmological model. Our results indicate that the CNN is highly resilient to these factors, with the exception of foregrounds, which can degrade performance by approximately 20%. Consequently, we conclude that this deep learning technique offers a promising alternative to traditional mass estimation methods.

This paper investigates how varying tokenization strategies influence the performance of Dirichlet Latent Allocation (LDA) models in text analysis. We evaluate three distinct strategies: word-based tokenization, collocation tokenization, and a hybrid approach combining both. Our findings indicate that collocation tokenization yields superior results compared to the other methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LDA models trained with collocation tokenization achieve higher topic consistency and interpretability, while also maintaining greater coherence and allocation across topics.

This study introduces a probabilistic classification framework for pulsars, which estimates the likelihood of each pulsar belonging to a specific population. The approach utilizes a hidden Markov model (HMM) to represent the underlying emission profiles of distinct pulsar classes. The HMM parameters are inferred from data using variational Bayes methods, and class membership probabilities are subsequently derived from these learned parameters. The method is validated through simulations on synthetic pulsar signals and further applied to the real dataset from the Parkes Pulsar Drift Survey.
